transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I’m here because... honestly, it’s just been exhausting, and I need someone to actually listen to me. For months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern playing out, and it’s not just a coincidence, no matter what anyone tries to tell me. I supervise an administrative office, you see, so I know exactly what normal clerical errors look like, and I know how offices are run. This is not that. 

It started with my sister’s appointments. Suddenly, they’re getting moved around or canceled without anyone consulting me. And then the bills—they keep showing up wrong, with these inexplicable discrepancies that make absolutely no sense. And when I try to get to the bottom of it, suddenly everyone just "forgets" to call me back. The receptionists, the billing departments, even my own family members... they just conveniently forget. 

They all just smile and patronize me and say, "Oh, it’s just a mistake, things slip through the cracks, you're overthinking it." But I know better. I can see exactly what they’re doing. They are deliberately keeping information from me. They’re coordinating this to try and push me out of all the important decisions, and they think I’m just going to sit back and let it happen, but I see the pattern clear as day.
Have you ever heard voices or whispers when there was no one around to make them?

Voices? Like... no, absolutely not. I know exactly what you’re getting at with a question like that, Doctor, and let me be perfectly clear: my mind is entirely sound. I don’t hear imaginary things, I don't hear ghosts or... or disembodied whispers in empty rooms. I am a very practical woman, I deal in facts and spreadsheets and administrative realities. 

What I *do* hear, however, are very real whispers from very real people who just think I’m out of earshot. Like just last Thursday, for instance. I went down to the clinic in person because they had completely bungled the billing code on my sister's account again—shocking, I know—and the moment I walked up to the reception desk, the two women sitting there immediately dropped their voices. They were whispering to each other, looking right at me, and then one of them suddenly picked up a stack of clipboards and scurried off to the back room while the other gave me that exact same fake, patronizing smile I was just telling you about. 

So, no, I don't hear things in my head. I hear what people are actually doing behind my back, the hushed tones they use when they’re caught off guard and have to quickly get their stories straight before dealing with me. I have excellent hearing, actually, which is probably why they find me so frustrating to deal with. In my own office, I always tell my staff that if you have something to say about a procedure, you say it at a normal volume, but these people at the clinic and the billing office, they operate entirely in these little secretive side-conversations. It's incredibly unprofessional, but it's certainly not a hallucination.
Throughout your adult life, have you generally felt that most people cannot be trusted?

Oh, no, no, not at all. Honestly, if you look at my track record, I’ve been managing people for... well, it has to be over thirty years now. You simply don't get to be a supervisor by walking around thinking everyone is out to get you. It just wouldn't work. In fact, a very large part of my job—probably the most important part, really—is delegating tasks and trusting that my team will actually execute them properly. 

When I hire a new administrative assistant, for example, I don't sit there scrutinizing their every move, assuming they're going to, I don't know, steal office supplies or lie on their timesheets. I give them the benefit of the doubt. I train them, I hand them the procedure manual—which I actually completely rewrote back in 2018 to make it more streamlined, because the old one was an absolute disaster—and I trust them to do the work. So, no, I am not a naturally suspicious person. I’ve always believed that people are generally decent and want to do a good job. I have friends I’ve known since I got my bachelor's degree, we get together regularly, we share everything. And I trusted my family completely. Completely! 

Which is exactly why this whole situation with my sister's accounts and the clinic has been such a terrible shock to the system. It’s not like I walked into this expecting them to be deceitful. I walked in expecting standard professional courtesy. I expected competence. But when you see the exact same "mistakes" happening over and over, and... and you see the whispering at the front desk, and you experience the deliberate exclusion from decisions... well, you'd have to be a fool to just keep trusting them blindly after that. But prior to this? Throughout my life? No, I’ve always been a very open, trusting person. Probably a bit too trusting, honestly, given how easily they thought they could pull the wool over my eyes.
